speaker: Phil Hufford
words: All right, today is Wednesday, July 5, and I am talking with Paula Elofson-Gardine, and we're going to be talking about Rocky Flats, and who knows what else.  Perhaps, perhaps we should start with the extent of the contamination that exists around Rocky Flats, and here I'm thinking of the soil contamination in particular, but you might want to just fill our listeners in on some of the other types of contamination also that exist outside the perimeters of the plant itself.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Okay, first of all, I'd like to state that I'm the director for Concerned Health Technicians for Cleaner Colorado. The reports that we have researched and compared with different sources have indicated that the contamination is extremely severe. We've had people from other contaminated areas tell us that our contamination here makes Three Mile Island look like National Park Service land, and I tend to believe that at this point, where the state standard for plutonium in soil is two disintegrations per minute, that is a radiological measure of activity per gram of soil, and this was arbitrarily set by an unqualified individual at the time to be that of 25 times background level, and this is basically to protect industry rather than the public. Despite that particular issue, the contamination levels off site at Rocky Flats from EPA information 12 years ago is 10 times that of the off-site contamination at the Nevada Test Site Area, and I think that that's enough to startle almost anybody. The state standard is a particular issue because, as John Gofman and Alice Stewart and many others have testified to there are no safe levels, at least to set any particular standard greater than background is ludicrous, and that there is a serious issue here, in that there should not be legally permissible levels of pollution, is what Dr. John Gofman is very concerned about this ties in with how hot is hot out at the plant. Some of the areas that are close to off site near the east fence by Indiana Street are severe enough that it is up to 8000 disintegrations per minute per gram of soil. This is we mainly plutonium, and that is certainly not the only toxic that they deal with out at the plant. They have quite a number of transuranics and volatile organic compounds. Those concentrations are out of this world in the 881 hillside area. This is an extreme concern because of the VOC plume going towards the reservoirs, and this is a prime concern, as far as EPA is concerned, that they want to see cleaned up. The other areas that are extremely hot, one of which is the solar evaporation ponds, have been used for process waste and act as a concentrating mechanism as this waste is evaporated. The sludge from these evaporated ponds is what they have used to make their pond crete out of this is a quaint little term they like to use because this is the sludge out of the ponds, so we'll mix it with concrete and call it pond crete. Well, this is the stuff that they had numerous accidents with in spills, and it was interesting to note, in reviewing the solar evaporation reports, that they had contamination in that sludge that was in the vicinity of 1,892,000 disintegrations per minute, I fail to see how that qualifies as low level radiation.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: When you say pond crete, are these solid blocks or is this a slurry, or what is that?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: They were intended to be solid blocks, but Rockwell had a problem with their recipe for concrete, and it ended up being the consistency of mayonnaise, which is why the containers collapsed and fell all over. Well, they only had a couple of them fall, but they had a significant problem with, I'd say, somewhere around 10,000 of these blocks that they were trying to make, then these triple layer cardboard boxes lined with plastic and it's just, it's laughable how they mismanaged it, and it's tragic at the same time that in asking them about decontamination procedures after spills, they very blithely laughed it off as it's no big deal, that stuff is pretty innocuous, we just threw a bucket of water on it, and it's decontaminated now, and we found that to be incredible, that they have such a lackadaisical attitude about what they're working with and how serious it is.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: So, what happened to all of this on the plant? Was it shipped off site?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: The concept was to solidify it and send it off to another storage facility, and they have begun shipping it out at this point. Those that have been stabilized, there is a problem with volatile organics in this particular sludge in this form that they're trying to make, and you cannot get solid concrete with volatile organics, so that is one of the problems out there. The liquids in these ponds have contamination in the vicinity of 123,000 disintegrations per minute, so you can see this stuff likes to cling to sediments and soils. The far greater hazard out there at the plant that is available to the public is the resuspended transuranic dust. This hangs in the atmosphere because of the unique characterization of this site. They have, excuse me, a complexing chemical complexing of plutonium with the volatile organics. This is chemicals like carbon tetrachloride solvents they use to clean machines, lathe oil, all that kind of stuff. And what happens is that as the stuff degrades and it's in the atmosphere, it creates a form of dispersed plutonium that can pass easily through any filters that are point 01 micron in size, and it's quite startling to many of the scientists that we discuss this with, because it tells them that it is so easily dispersed and so serious that it is much lighter than the atmosphere, so it remains hanging in suspension in the atmosphere out there in pretty great concentrations with levels between 4,000 and 8,000 disintegrations per minute, and the problem we have here is that this remains available for human ingestion and inhalation pathways.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: So this is an ongoing process. I mean, these particles are being emitted as we speak, and are being blown over the Denver metropolitan area. Is that right?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: That's precisely what's happening. They have a number of different kinds of incinerators out there, and they emit on a daily basis, regardless of inversions or anything else, one of the more serious problems out at the plant is what has already been put out into the soil, the 903 pad, where they in the past had such poor grasp of what they were doing out there that they literally were just dumping this stuff, and this is a large amount of where some of this resuspension originated from, and it is a horrible mess out there that people need to stay away from.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: How extensive is the contamination, the airborne contamination. How far does that reach? I mean, is most of it hit hit the ground around Arvada or Westminster, or does it go to Washington DC? What, what is the pattern of this contamination fallout?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Well, the fallout, the problem is it does not settle out. Like I said before. It remains clinging into the atmosphere, it clings to air particulates, making our brown cloud radioactive. I conferred with a meteorologist about this, and his feeling was once it's been atmospherically dispersed around the primary area, which I'd say we all get it pretty much, not in such heavy concentrations. It is going to be more dispersed. It's like stray bullets, you might get it, you might not. But his feeling was that as the greater winds aloft go, they probably have a greater concentration of this ending up in Greeley and Fort Collins.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Really, really, it's not necessarily the Denver metro area that's getting the brunt of it then.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Well, we certainly get our major share of it, but as the particulates and the emissions go higher up into the atmosphere, it's carried farther up the valley, but we do have a concentrating effect because of our unique topography here.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: So, the bulk of the emissions are coming out of the top of smokestacks out there? Or, what are the sources? Ground level?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Well, you have both, I guess, for lack of better terms, you could call them smokestacks, but they're much more sophisticated than that. This goes into issues about the HEPA filters and their supposed efficiencies, that is touted by the DOE, the Department of Energy, but they are found to be grossly deficient because of the size of the particles that pass on through, and the alpha recoil effect, which energizes the particles, and then they go out with much greater force. So you have a number of different issues that come into play there about what really is coming out of the stack, and this is something that does get into the upper atmosphere. I'd say the monitoring system out there is a joke. It is completely and wholly inadequate. Having perimeter samplers, obviously, if this stuff is going out at several hundred feet over the ground, it's not going to settle out till it's far past those monitors.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: If you would go into a little bit more detail on this alpha recoil effect.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: The best that I could do would be to quote a friend who's been involved with the issue, Agua Das, in his testimony to the Ahearne Commission, which was the Advisory Committee on Nuclear Facility Safety, back in March of '89 he described the alpha recoil effect to these physicists, and they loved it. He talked about the filtering and sampling methods, and the limitations... that an alpha particle is like a helium nucleus, it's big and it travels with a lot of inertia, like an elephant shot out of a slingshot, and that it has a tremendous amount of momentum that is imparted, like jumping out of a boat, and the momentum that is imparted is capable of fracturing small submicron particles off particles off the surface of a piece of plutonium metal, also any spills they have that dries up the alpha disintegration can re-entrain those materials from the dried spills. This, these little submicron particles that are splintered off make it through those filters with the greatest of ease. Okay, that's the point. That the filters are inadequate, they're supposed to be quote 99.99% effective, but the simple fact is it's like shoveling a bunch of gravel down a big hole. This stuff gets right through, and it's the respirable variety that's really dangerous to human life.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: These ponds, is there any evaporation of transuranic material from the ponds or volatile organic compounds from these solar ponds?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Well, I understand that there's been problems with cracks in the liners, that there has been seepage from these ponds. This is a big problem that is a concern to EPA, and I have to assume to the CDH as well, although I have my doubts that this has Colorado Department of Health, we have some deep concerns about their role in the situation here, that they have not protected the public health as they should have. I think that it's been a problem in their radiological division with having qualified people. We're very concerned that the state standard was set by an individual who was not a radio biophysicist and someone of the stature of Dr. Edward Martell would have been more appropriate to be the person to take care of that particular issue. The plume they have from the solar evaporation ponds I would consider to be hot waste and it's something that they don't have a handle on at this point in time, and the Newsweek reporter saying that this was like a creeping Chernobyl, I believe, is absolutely on the button.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Now, when you say a plume, what are you referring to here?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Well, this is what people call, okay, if you watered your, your lawn, and you hit a dry patch, and you had liquid going down into the dirt, you'd have kind of like a head to it, okay, where you have the beginning part of the wetness that goes down into the dirt, it's like that, it's a plume of wetness or a plume of chemicals.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: I see, so you're talking about a plume of water or of waterborne waste, as opposed to an airborne plume of particles.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Yes, you can have a number of different ways of utilizing that term. Plumes in the air, we've conferred with meteorologists about what they're putting out and where it goes, some of this stuff does settle out on the reservoirs and around the land around the plant, and it's just this place does not belong near a large community. I'm not sure if it belongs anywhere from that point matter, but it is such a huge mess. It's been basically an unregulated, filthy smelting operation that deals with extremely dangerous and toxic radionuclides and other substances for over 35 years, and we see the results of that. It may take decades to clean it up, the clean up may be worse than the original pollution, because of the resuspension and the problems kicking up all of this contamination once again. So, we've only seen the beginning, and the first point of this is, they must close that place. As long as they continue to operate and add to the pollution. They're making it that much harder to clean up. You can't have cleanup as long as they're continuing to emit.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Can you speak a little bit more about role of the Colorado Department of Health in monitoring and controlling the plant? Have there been any violations of permits, are there any permitted releases of materials? You might talk a little bit about the drinking water supplies, Standley Lake, Great Western Reservoir.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Okay, we have hazardous materials division and radiological division people that have been, let's say, studying the issue. I would never say they are controlling the plant. I believe it's been uncontrollable for many years, too many years. The soil sediment and studies done on Standley Lake showed that it is a problem, they have, they have significant amounts of contamination in the sediments, you have lake turnover that happens twice a year, and all of this stuff is resuspended in the water. I believe that these bodies of water, Great Western and Standley, should not be used ever for public drinking supplies. I think that the current water sampling is inadequate. I think that if they do not have measurements from the source, they don't really know what's out there or where it's gone to, and the sediments play a very stringent role in that, in the banks, and in the actual sediment of the lakes, we have had discourse with people from the School of Mines that have studied it, and they've been very alarmed at it. We've also talked to people at Argonne National Labs who have knowledge of the situation out here, and they say these are the most polluted waterways in the country, and they are very alarmed at the levels that are out here, and I frankly do not believe the information the health department is releasing on what they say they're finding. There's something very wrong with this picture.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: The health department claims that the sediment bearing the plutonium contamination is stable and does not get resuspended, and that the contamination was due to a couple of events, the fire in 1957 and the 1969 fire, and therefore, since the plutonium is tightly bound to soil and other particles, that there is no current danger to the drinking water quality. Do you agree with that?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: No, I don't. I don't agree with it at all. Plutonium is not the only problem out there, and as it's in the environment, it will degrade. Americium is a much more serious threat. It is much more toxic, it's more readily taken up by the body, and it is more radioactive than plutonium. So, the americium question has not been addressed. They run from those questions. The uranium situation out there is likewise severe. Rocky Flats puts out a lot of uranium. This puts out a lot of radon. They calibrate their monitors against radon and thorium. Those are all alpha emitters. I think that it's a very serious situation, where a full characterization of that plant has never been done, and I think that this leaves a very large question mark in terms of public health and safety, that our interests, our needs have not been met by our current CDH people, and I think that there should be a turnover there. Dr. Tom Vernon has been repeatedly the crux of the problem with the governor. In public meetings, we've asked him this, and in other forums, and he has repeatedly said to the governor, quote, there's no problem at Rocky Flats. Well, he's also said there's no problem at Martin Marietta, no problem at the Arsenal, no problem at the Lowry landfill. He is a problem. He is the problem. This man is trained in epidemiology extensively, that is almost the complete extent of his training, which is very appropriate for a director of the Department of Health, but he is not environmentally trained, and he is not qualified to say there is no problem if he cannot step down and resign because of this crisis of waste in the state of Colorado, and the CDH's failure to be responding appropriately, then we need a co-director that comes with from a place that is not in Colorado without vested interest in this state we have too much dirty politicking going on in the state that includes polluters being a part of health boards such as Richard Newman from Thoreau being on the Jefferson County Board of Health, who hounded Dr. Carl Johnson out of his job because he tried to make the public aware of what happened out there at Rocky Flats. It's a chemical company that supplied chemicals to Dow and then to Rockwell. It's very inappropriate to have the polluters be taking part in the regulators or vice versa. And I think that we have a very serious problem in this state that demands an outside investigation, and to shake this up we've got to get rid of these people that have been a part of the problem.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: So do you think that it's a matter of Vernon not being properly educated, not being trained in how serious the situation is from a medical standpoint, or do you think that there might actually be some type of collusion that he knows what's going on, but is just minimizing it and trivializing it to protect business interests and to keep the state attractive for new business growth?

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: I think that both of those are very true. I couldn't have said it any better than you did right there. I think that we have a very serious problem with people with vested interest in the state of Colorado. I think the public has a right to know, and my statement would be this. Who are you, Tom Vernon or Al Hazel, to tell everyone that plutonium isn't toxic, or that everything's a-okay here? The public has a right to know, and the public may be alarmed at what's going on here, and they darn well should be. They have been lied to, and this has been covered up for too long. Maybe it is alarming to the public, and they've been trying to avoid public panic, but had they played a more responsible role in the last 20 years, we would not have a problem that would be this extensive at this point in time.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: How about the plans of the city of Arvada to annex land directly south of the Rocky Flats nuclear weapons plant as the first phase of an extensive development to be called the Jefferson Center. Can you enlighten our listeners as to what's involved in that?

words: I'd be happy to. I don't know when you'll air this, but taped a show last week with United Cable. I think that it is a ludicrous plan that is really tragic, that these people are so greedy for money that they will develop at any cost. Mr. Lacey used to be a DOE engineer.

speaker: Phil Hufford
words: Yes. Explain who the people are.

speaker: Paula Elofson-Gardine
words: Mr. Lacey is one of the lead developers who also sits on the board of W470 Authority. He is also the head of the Jefferson County Associates. He used to be very tightly interwoven with Department of Energy. He knows very well what's out there, and the attitude Mr. Lacey has is there is nothing wrong, we can go ahead and develop out here, and it's very indicative of the malaise in general of Department of Energy and Rockwell people that have a lackadaisical attitude about the seriousness and the extent of the contamination out there. They have used the argument that the levels of contamination are quote within the state standard. That's not very comforting in light of the fact that the state standard does not mean that it's harmless, and people need to realize that because something is within a certain standard doesn't mean that it's harmless, no matter what it is. So, if we had everything in our water that the Clean Water Act said we could have, we'd all be dropping like flies here, and I think that this is something people need to take into consideration, that if the Church McCain land was contaminated to the extent that they were given a multi million dollar out-of-court settlement from the federal government for contamination from the previous serious incidents at Rocky Flats. What makes it okay now if plutonium has a half life of 24,000 years? It is still out there. It has not been remediated or removed. There have been pitiful attempts at plowing, which only disperses it farther, and the state standard was set so that it was applied to virgin undisturbed soil only, not land that had been plowed and dispersed, and the state standard was erroneously set for plutonium when the screening level guide from the EPA was for total transuranics, not just plutonium, so there are errors in that whole method, and the Department of health did a, how do you say it, a backup document three years after the plutonium standard was set to justify a dose risk assessment argument, which I believe is a sham. It still doesn't, it still does not make what they did okay.
